name: Monic
region: Lower Myanmar (Mon State) and central Thailand
defining_innovation: Mon and Nyahkur, languages of the early Buddhist kingdoms of lower Myanmar and central Thailand, whose script became the model for Burmese writing.

chapters.title: Dvaravati and Old Mon
chapters.body: Mon was the language of some of the earliest Buddhist states of mainland Southeast Asia: the Dvaravati culture of central Thailand (6th–11th centuries) and the kingdoms of lower Burma around Thaton and Pegu. Old Mon inscriptions from the 6th–7th centuries are among the oldest texts in any Austroasiatic language. Nyahkur, spoken by a few thousand people in central Thailand, is thought to be a remnant of Dvaravati Mon.

chapters.title: Teacher of Burma
chapters.body: When the Burmese kingdom of Pagan rose in the 11th century, it adopted Theravada Buddhism and the Mon script from its Mon neighbours. The Myazedi inscription (1113) records the same text in Pali, Mon, Burmese and Pyu. Burmese took many Mon words and some grammatical patterns. In later centuries the balance shifted. After the Burmese king Alaungpaya destroyed the Mon capital, Pegu, in 1757, many Mon fled to Thailand, and in Myanmar Mon speakers have been shifting to Burmese ever since.

turning_points.title: Old Mon inscriptions
turning_points.description: Mon inscriptions in a script of southern Indian origin appear in central Thailand and lower Burma, recording Buddhist donations.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: Mon script and Burmese
turning_points.description: The Burmese of Pagan adopt Theravada Buddhism and the Mon script, and the Myazedi inscription of 1113 sets Mon beside Pali, Burmese and Pyu. Burmese takes Mon vocabulary into religion, administration and daily life.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.

turning_points.title: The fall of Pegu
turning_points.description: Alaungpaya's destruction of the Mon kingdom leads to flight into Thailand and a long shift from Mon to Burmese in Myanmar. Mon survives today in Mon State and in communities in Thailand.

sources.citation: Jenny, Mathias & Paul Sidwell, eds. 2015. The Handbook of Austroasiatic Languages. Leiden: Brill.
